C_product_page_copy.short_product_summary: Reduced Glutathione (GSH) is a small tripeptide — glutamate, cysteine, and glycine — that functions as the primary low-molecular-weight thiol in cellular biochemistry. It exists in two interconvertible redox forms: reduced glutathione (GSH, the thiol form) and oxidized glutathione (GSSG, the disulfide). Veracue supplies the reduced form (GSH, CAS 70-18-8, MW 307.32 g/mol) as a research-grade chemical for laboratory and in vitro use. It is not intended for human consumption, veterinary use, diagnostic procedures, or therapeutic application.

product_description.overview:
Glutathione is one of the most studied small molecules in redox biology and cellular biochemistry. The reduced form — GSH — is the biologically active thiol species and the dominant form found in healthy cells. It donates electrons to reduce reactive oxygen species, is recycled back from its oxidized form (GSSG) by glutathione reductase using NADPH, and acts as a substrate for the glutathione S-transferase (GST) enzyme family, which catalyzes conjugation of electrophilic compounds to facilitate excretion. That three-part role — redox buffer, direct radical scavenger, and xenobiotic conjugation substrate — makes it a central molecule in cellular oxidative-stress research, enzyme-activity studies, and GSH/GSSG ratio measurements.

For procurement and research planning purposes, the distinction between GSH and GSSG is not minor. They are different chemical entities with different molecular weights (307.32 vs 612.63 g/mol), different CAS numbers (70-18-8 vs 27025-41-8), and different analytical behavior. Supplier pages that list 'Glutathione' without specifying the redox form create procurement ambiguity. Veracue's product is the reduced form.

chemical_identity_section.heading: Chemical Identity of Reduced Glutathione (GSH)
chemical_identity_section.body: Reduced glutathione (GSH) is a tripeptide synthesized from three amino acids: L-glutamate, L-cysteine, and glycine. The glutamate-cysteine bond is a γ-glutamyl linkage — an unusual bond at the side-chain carboxyl group of glutamate rather than the alpha-carboxyl — which makes glutathione resistant to most peptidases. The cysteine-glycine bond is a standard peptide bond. The free thiol (–SH) on cysteine is what gives GSH its redox activity.

gsh_vs_gssg_section.heading: GSH and GSSG Are Different Chemical Entities
gsh_vs_gssg_section.body:
Reduced glutathione (GSH) and oxidized glutathione (GSSG) are not the same compound. GSSG forms when two GSH molecules are linked via a disulfide bond at their cysteine residues during oxidation. The result is a substantially different molecule: twice the molecular weight, a different CAS number, and a different structural form. In a living cell, the enzyme glutathione reductase converts GSSG back to two molecules of GSH using NADPH — that recycling cycle is what maintains the intracellular GSH/GSSG ratio as a measure of redox state.

In research supply, the two are sold as separate products. A COA that does not explicitly specify 'reduced' or 'oxidized' — or that does not provide a CAS number to resolve the ambiguity — should be scrutinized before procurement.

rows: Product of GSH oxidation; recycled by glutathione reductase
Redox studies, antioxidant assays, enzyme-system research

biochemical_research_context_section.heading: What Glutathione Does in Biochemical Research
biochemical_research_context_section.body:
Glutathione's biochemical roles are well-established at the mechanistic level. Three are worth understanding in research context:

Redox buffering: GSH donates electrons to reduce hydrogen peroxide and lipid peroxides, becoming GSSG in the process. The intracellular GSH/GSSG ratio — typically heavily weighted toward GSH in healthy cells — is used in oxidative-stress research as an index of cellular redox state. Glutathione reductase regenerates GSH from GSSG using NADPH, completing the cycle.

Thiol chemistry and direct scavenging: The free –SH group on cysteine reacts directly with electrophiles and reactive species. Glutathione peroxidases use GSH as a cofactor to reduce peroxides, with GSH oxidized to GSSG as a byproduct. This enzyme-mediated pathway is a major line of antioxidant defense studied in redox biology.

Conjugation and detoxification: Glutathione S-transferases (GSTs) catalyze the conjugation of GSH to electrophilic xenobiotics and reactive metabolites, forming more water-soluble products that can be excreted. This is one of the central mechanisms studied in drug metabolism and toxicological research.

Important boundary: These are biochemical mechanisms with strong in vitro and in vivo evidence. They describe what GSH does at the molecular and cellular level. They are not claims that Veracue's research material treats, cures, or prevents any disease or condition in humans.

enzyme_systems_reference.glutathione_peroxidase: Uses GSH to reduce H₂O₂ and lipid peroxides; generates GSSG
enzyme_systems_reference.glutathione_reductase: Recycles GSSG back to two GSH molecules; requires NADPH
enzyme_systems_reference.glutathione_s_transferases: Conjugate GSH to electrophilic substrates; multiple isoforms with different substrate specificities
enzyme_systems_reference.gamma_glutamylcysteine_ligase: Rate-limiting enzyme in GSH biosynthesis; converts glutamate + cysteine to γ-glutamylcysteine
enzyme_systems_reference.glutathione_synthetase: Adds glycine to γ-glutamylcysteine to complete GSH synthesis

research_applications_section.heading: Research Contexts Where GSH Is Studied
research_applications_section.body:
Reduced glutathione is used across several areas of biochemical and cell-biology research. These include:

Oxidative stress and redox biology: Measuring the GSH/GSSG ratio in cell or tissue samples as a redox-state indicator. Studying how oxidative challenges shift that ratio and how cells recover GSH levels.

Thiol chemistry and enzyme kinetics: Studying glutathione peroxidase and glutathione reductase activity, substrate binding, and inhibition profiles.

Xenobiotic and drug metabolism research: Investigating GST-mediated conjugation pathways for electrophilic compounds in in vitro metabolism models.

Analytical methodology development: GSH is used as a reference standard for HPLC and LC-MS method development and validation in bioanalytical research.

GSH/GSSG ratio assays: Developing and validating assays that quantify both forms simultaneously — requiring derivatization strategies (e.g., NEM-trapping of GSH) to prevent pre-analytic oxidation artifacts.

None of these applications constitute therapeutic use. This product is not intended for administration to humans or animals.

analytical_verification_section.heading: How Glutathione Research Materials Are Analytically Tested
analytical_verification_section.body: Two analytical methods are most commonly used to characterize glutathione research materials: HPLC and LC-MS. They measure different things, and understanding the difference matters for reading a COA correctly.

coa_interpretation_guidance.heading: What a Glutathione COA Should Contain
coa_interpretation_guidance.body: A rigorous COA for a glutathione research material should document: (1) product identity confirming the specific redox form (GSH or GSSG) with the correct CAS number, (2) purity/assay percentage by HPLC with a chromatogram or reference to the method used, (3) molecular identity confirmation by LC-MS with the expected and observed mass, (4) lot or batch number and test date, (5) analytical method details sufficient to assess the method's appropriateness, and (6) laboratory identification. A COA that provides a purity figure without specifying the redox form or identifying the analytical method gives less information than it appears to.

stability_and_handling_section.heading: Why Glutathione Stability Matters in Research
stability_and_handling_section.body:
Reduced glutathione (GSH) is chemically reactive at its thiol group — which is both what makes it biologically important and what makes it susceptible to oxidation during storage and handling. Exposure to oxygen, light, moisture, and elevated temperature can convert GSH to GSSG, producing a materially different compound. In solution, oxidation proceeds faster than in solid form. Repeated freeze-thaw cycles can also accelerate degradation.

These are general scientific principles governing thiol chemistry. They are not a substitute for Veracue's product-specific storage instructions, which will reflect the exact form, packaging, and validated stability data for this product. [Veracue storage instructions to be supplied and published here.]

For researchers working with reconstituted glutathione: sample preparation for GSH/GSSG measurement typically requires immediate derivatization (e.g., with N-ethylmaleimide) to trap GSH and prevent pre-analytic oxidation artifacts in the assay. This is an analytical consideration, not a Veracue product protocol.

research_use_boundary_section.heading: Research Use Only
research_use_boundary_section.body:
Veracue's Reduced Glutathione (GSH) is manufactured and sold exclusively for in vitro laboratory and preclinical research. It is not a drug, dietary supplement, cosmetic, or food product. It is not approved by the FDA or any regulatory body for human or veterinary therapeutic use. No FDA-approved glutathione drug product exists in the United States. FDA and CDC have issued advisories specifically regarding injectable glutathione compounded from non-injectable ingredients for wellness or skin-lightening purposes — Veracue's research material has no connection to those applications.

This product must not be administered to humans or animals outside a properly licensed research facility. Nothing on this page constitutes medical advice. Buyers confirm they are qualified researchers, laboratories, or institutions acquiring this material for lawful research purposes, and accept full responsibility for compliance with applicable regulations.

faqs.question: What is glutathione?
faqs.answer: Glutathione is a tripeptide composed of three amino acids — L-glutamate, L-cysteine, and glycine — linked by a γ-glutamyl bond between glutamate and cysteine, and a standard peptide bond between cysteine and glycine. It exists in two interconvertible redox forms: reduced glutathione (GSH, the thiol form) and oxidized glutathione (GSSG, the disulfide). In biochemical research, 'glutathione' most commonly refers to the reduced form (GSH) unless otherwise specified.

faqs.question: What is reduced glutathione (GSH)?
faqs.answer: Reduced glutathione (GSH) is the thiol form of glutathione — the form containing a free sulfhydryl (–SH) group on the cysteine residue. This is the biologically active redox species: the –SH group is what GSH uses to donate electrons to reactive oxygen species, to serve as a substrate for glutathione peroxidases and S-transferases, and to function as the primary low-molecular-weight intracellular antioxidant. Its CAS number is 70-18-8 and its molecular weight is 307.32 g/mol.

faqs.question: What is the difference between GSH and GSSG?
faqs.answer: GSH (reduced glutathione) and GSSG (oxidized glutathione / glutathione disulfide) are distinct chemical entities. GSSG forms when two GSH molecules are oxidized and their cysteine thiols form a disulfide bond. The two compounds have different molecular formulas (C₁₀H₁₇N₃O₆S for GSH; C₂₀H₃₂N₆O₁₂S₂ for GSSG), different molecular weights (307.32 vs 612.63 g/mol), and different CAS numbers (70-18-8 vs 27025-41-8). In research use, they are procured and documented separately. Conflating them in a protocol or a COA is a meaningful scientific error.

faqs.question: What is the molecular weight of reduced glutathione?
faqs.answer: The molecular weight of reduced glutathione (GSH) is 307.32 g/mol. Its molecular formula is C₁₀H₁₇N₃O₆S and its CAS number is 70-18-8. The oxidized form (GSSG) has a molecular weight of 612.63 g/mol — approximately double, because GSSG is a dimer of two GSH units linked by a disulfide bond. Using the wrong molecular weight in a reconstitution or assay calculation will produce incorrect concentrations.

faqs.question: What is the CAS number for reduced glutathione?
faqs.answer: The CAS number for reduced L-glutathione (GSH) is 70-18-8. Its PubChem CID is 124886. The oxidized form (GSSG) has a different CAS number: 27025-41-8. When verifying a research material purchase, confirming the CAS number on the COA is the fastest way to establish which form the documentation actually applies to.

faqs.question: Is glutathione a peptide?
faqs.answer: Yes. Glutathione is a tripeptide — a short peptide made of three amino acid residues. It is significantly smaller than most research peptides (MW 307.32 g/mol), and its γ-glutamyl linkage makes it structurally unusual compared to conventional peptides. In research and chemical supply, it is classified both as a peptide and as a small-molecule thiol, depending on the context. Veracue categorizes it as a research chemical, consistent with its use in biochemical and analytical research rather than as a conventional long-chain synthetic peptide.

faqs.question: What does glutathione do in biochemical research?
faqs.answer: The three most-studied roles of GSH in biochemical research are: (1) redox buffering — GSH donates electrons to reduce reactive oxygen species and peroxides, becoming GSSG; the GSH/GSSG ratio is used as a cellular redox-state index; (2) enzyme substrate — glutathione peroxidases use GSH to reduce H₂O₂ and lipid peroxides, and glutathione reductase recycles GSSG back to GSH using NADPH; (3) xenobiotic conjugation — glutathione S-transferases (GSTs) catalyze the attachment of GSH to electrophilic compounds, which is a primary mechanism studied in drug-metabolism and toxicology research. These are established biochemical mechanisms, not claims about therapeutic benefit in humans.

faqs.question: What does HPLC show for a glutathione research material?
faqs.answer: High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) measures chromatographic purity — the percentage of the detected signal attributed to the main peak, under the analytical method used. A high HPLC purity figure (e.g., ≥98% or ≥99%) indicates that the majority of the material elutes as a single species under those conditions. What HPLC does not establish on its own is molecular identity: a high purity number does not confirm the compound is GSH rather than GSSG or another related thiol. Identity confirmation requires mass spectrometry (LC-MS) or comparison to a certified reference standard.

faqs.question: What does LC-MS show for a glutathione research material?
faqs.answer: Liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC-MS) measures the mass of molecules eluting from the column. For a reduced glutathione sample, LC-MS should detect a molecular ion consistent with GSH (MW 307.32 Da). This confirms molecular identity and is the most direct way to distinguish GSH from GSSG (MW 612.63 Da). LC-MS identity confirmation and HPLC purity assessment answer different questions — both matter for a complete analytical picture. A sample can have high HPLC purity while being the wrong compound; LC-MS rules that out.

faqs.question: How can reduced glutathione be distinguished from oxidized glutathione analytically?
faqs.answer: The most reliable method is LC-MS: GSH (307.32 Da) and GSSG (612.63 Da) have different masses and are directly distinguishable. HPLC with an appropriate method can also separate the two chromatographically when reference standards are available. In biological sample analysis, derivatization agents such as N-ethylmaleimide (NEM) are used to trap and stabilize GSH before analysis, preventing further oxidation to GSSG during sample preparation — a critical step for accurate GSH/GSSG ratio measurements. In powder purity testing, the distinction is most cleanly made by LC-MS identity confirmation alongside the HPLC purity run.

faqs.question: What should researchers look for in a glutathione COA?
faqs.answer: A rigorous COA for a glutathione research material should include: (1) the specific redox form (GSH or GSSG) with the correct CAS number — this alone resolves the most common entity ambiguity; (2) a purity/assay result by HPLC (with a chromatogram or explicit method reference); (3) molecular identity confirmation by LC-MS; (4) lot or batch number and test date for traceability; (5) the testing laboratory and method details. A COA that provides a purity figure without specifying the redox form, or without LC-MS identity confirmation, is less informative than it appears.

faqs.question: What should researchers verify before purchasing a glutathione research material?
faqs.answer: Before procurement, researchers should confirm: (1) the exact chemical form — is it GSH (CAS 70-18-8) or GSSG (CAS 27025-41-8)? The CAS number on the COA answers this; (2) purity by HPLC and identity confirmation by LC-MS are both present on the COA; (3) the lot number on the COA matches the lot being shipped; (4) the analytical method is appropriate — HPLC conditions should be capable of separating GSH from common impurities; (5) storage conditions are specified and compatible with your laboratory setup. Suppliers who clearly document the redox form, provide traceable batch COAs, and explain what their testing establishes are the ones worth working with.

Chemical identity of GSSG: CAS 27025-41-8, MW 612.63 g/mol, formula C₂₀H₃₂N₆O₁₂S₂ — confirmed against Sigma-Aldrich catalog and research literature
Tripeptide composition (glutamate, cysteine, glycine) and γ-glutamyl linkage — confirmed from PubChem and PMC biochemistry reviews
Biochemical roles (redox buffering, glutathione peroxidase/reductase systems, GST conjugation) — supported by PMC2696075 and PMC3422610
HPLC measures purity, not identity; LC-MS measures identity, not purity — confirmed from analytical method literature (PMC8598684)
No FDA-approved glutathione drug product in the United States — confirmed from CDC/FDA advisory references
GSH/GSSG distinction is chemically material (different MW, CAS, formula, behavior) — confirmed from multiple chemical database sources
Commercial marketplace defaults 'Glutathione' to reduced form (GSH) — confirmed from supplier terminology survey in research brief
what_remained_unavailable: Veracue-specific product form confirmation (GSH vs GSSG) — assumed GSH, must be confirmed

I_final_qa_report.major_seo_opportunity: Own the analytical disambiguation niche: HPLC vs LC-MS (what each establishes vs does not), GSH/GSSG form clarity, and COA interpretation guidance. No current competitor page explains all three cleanly in one place. This creates a compounding advantage — researchers who find this page for analytical questions are also the procurement-intent audience.
I_final_qa_report.major_geo_opportunity: Build an unambiguous entity graph: Glutathione → GSH (CAS 70-18-8, MW 307.32) → GSSG (CAS 27025-41-8, MW 612.63) → GSH/GSSG redox couple → glutathione peroxidase → glutathione reductase → glutathione S-transferases. The explicit CAS/MW anchors, comparison table, and enzyme-system reference give AI answer engines precise, citable entity relationships.
I_final_qa_report.major_aeo_opportunity: The FAQ and analytical section directly answer the 12 highest-priority questions (CAS, MW, HPLC vs LC-MS, what a COA should contain, how to distinguish GSH from GSSG) faster and more precisely than any existing vendor page in the research brief's SERP survey. Each FAQ answer follows the problem → direct answer → nuance/limitation model.
I_final_qa_report.major_scientific_caution: The GSH/GSSG redox cycle and enzyme-system roles are biochemical mechanisms with strong in vitro and in vivo evidence. They must never be extended to therapeutic claims about disease prevention, treatment, or health benefits in humans. The distinction between 'what GSH does in a cell' and 'what taking glutathione does for a person' must be maintained throughout any future edits to this page.
I_final_qa_report.major_regulatory_caution: No FDA-approved glutathione drug product exists. Injectable glutathione for wellness or skin-lightening is explicitly warned against by FDA/CDC. These regulatory facts apply to specific clinical or consumer-wellness uses, not universally to all glutathione research materials — but the page's RUO disclaimer and claim-boundary section must be preserved intact, and no future editor should add therapeutic, clinical, or wellness claims to this page without legal review.
I_final_qa_report.publish_readiness: NOT YET READY — Page copy, FAQ, and entity sections are complete and verified. The entity gate (GSH vs GSSG confirmation) must be resolved first.
